title: Square Counter
context: Grade 4, and the first time the chapter measures a space rather than a length. An adult sees squares being counted, which a child can do on squared paper. What is actually being settled is the unit: area counts squares, so it is written in square units, and a square one centimetre on every side gives a square centimetre. The page's own squared figures in the perimeter exercise were built so that no shape's perimeter equals its area, and a child who counts squares when asked for the edge gives a different number, which is why the two counts stand side by side here.

writeup.why: Cover a shape with equal squares and count the space inside it, then set that count beside the length of the edge round it.
writeup.look: A shape on a squared sheet, a tray of square tiles beside it, a counter at the top left of the canvas, and a compare bay at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Square Counter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the tiles laid, one number in ink, climbing by one as each tile snaps into place and never taking a tile that was handed back, with the unit card under it once it has been turned. On the third phase it carries the rows laid and the squares in one row beside the total, and on the fourth the squares inside only, the edge count being kept in the compare bay. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The squared sheet fills the left of the working area, 680 by 440 at 64,214, ruled in near-black squares, with a shape's boundary drawn along the grid lines in deep blue so that every square is wholly inside it or wholly outside it. The tile tray runs under the sheet, 680 by 56 at 64,666, holding equal green tiles the size of the sheet's own squares. A tile dragged onto the shape snaps edge to edge with its neighbours; a tile dropped across a gap or onto another tile springs back to the tray with the gap or the overlap lit where it was, and it is not counted. The unit card lies face down under the running count until it is turned, when it shows one square lifted out of the sheet with each side marked one centimetre, and reads square units or square centimetres. The compare bay stands at the right, 390 by 440 at 760,214, in two columns headed inside and round: the squares inside a shape, counted by its tiles, in green, and the edges round it, counted in amber by the edge walker, a small amber marker that goes round the outside one square's edge at a time. Two shapes can stand in the bay at once, each with its two counts under it. The rows control sits under the bay, 390 by 56 at 760,666: on a rectangle it fills the first row, then copies that row down one at a time, writing each new row's number at its left and the total so far beside it. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a count is asked for, with three unit keys under them reading square units, square centimetres and centimetres, so an area is written with its unit by press and the unit of a length stands beside it to be told apart. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion. A length being measured, walked, added or named, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted. The second thing set beside the first, a fold being tried, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter and the larger angle between clock hands, is sky blue. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a point is a round dot, a line carries an arrowhead at each end, a ray a dot and one arrowhead and a segment a dot at each end, a measured length carries its number, a hidden edge is dashed and a line of symmetry is dotted, before any of them is told by a colour. A dotted line always means a true line of symmetry or a mirror line, and a fold being tried is drawn solid until it is kept, so nothing else on any stage of this chapter is ever dotted. The squares inside a shape are always green and the edge round it always amber, so area and perimeter never share a colour on this stage, and they never share a unit. A tile is either wholly inside the shape or not laid at all, so no square is ever cut.
writeup.finish: The card shows the shape the child covered, its tiles in rows, and its area and perimeter standing side by side with their units.

phases.win: the last tile snaps in, the shape is covered edge to edge, and the count stands as its area in square units
phases.does: drags tiles onto the shape until it is covered, then reads the count
phases.goal: area is the space inside a boundary, counted in equal squares that leave no gaps and do not overlap
phases.says: Cover it with the squares. No gaps, and none on top of another.
phases.check: Away from the screen: cover a small book with paper squares of one size, edge to edge, and count them.
phases.feels: the squares have to meet edge to edge and stay inside the edge, or the count means nothing
phases.hands: Give each group a book and a pile of paper squares all cut to one size. Ask them to cover the cover edge to edge, with no gaps and none on top of another, and count. Then ask one group to leave a gap in the middle and another to overlap two squares, and ask whether either count is the space the cover takes up.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: is every tile inside the boundary? Second rung, the phase's: is there a gap or an overlap anywhere? Third rung: the shape is cut to a strip of three squares and covered tile by tile before the larger shape comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a count of tiles feels like the answer whatever the tiles are doing, and a tile is a tile wherever it lies.
wrong.move: leaves gaps between the tiles or lays one tile over another, and counts whatever is on the shape.
wrong.screen: the tile over the gap or on top of another springs back to the tray with the gap or the overlap lit where it sat, and the count does not take it. The tiles already laid stay where they are, the space still bare is drawn in outline so the covering can be finished edge to edge, and the child's count stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the whole sheet is squared, and every square on it looks like one of the equal squares the question is about.
wrong.move: counts every square of the sheet the shape sits on, instead of only the squares inside its boundary.
wrong.screen: the tiles inside the boundary glow green and the squares of the sheet outside it stay the plain panel colour, with the deep blue boundary lit between them. The tiles are counted again one row at a time, only inside the boundary, and the child's larger number stays in the slot beside the new count.

phases.screen: a shape on the sheet and a tray of equal square tiles beside it
phases.soWhat: Area is the space inside a boundary, counted in equal squares with no gaps and no overlaps.

phases.win: the unit card turns to square centimetres and settles beside the count
phases.does: counts the shaded squares, then turns the unit card and writes the area with its unit
phases.goal: a square one centimetre on every side gives a square centimetre, the unit of area
phases.says: Each square is one centimetre on every side. What unit is the area in?
phases.check: On centimetre squared paper, shade a shape of six squares. Write its area with its unit.
phases.feels: the unit is a square, so the answer counts squares and says so
phases.hands: Draw a square one centimetre on each side with a ruler, cut it out and call it one square centimetre. Lay it on a shape drawn on centimetre squared paper and count how many times it fits. Ask what unit the answer should carry, and why centimetres alone is not enough.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many squares are shaded? Second rung, the phase's: what is the size of each square? Third rung: the grid is cut to one shaded square, and the unit card is turned over it before the larger shape comes back. The number pad and the unit keys stay open.

wrong.why: the perimeters just before this were in centimetres, and the grid is marked one centimetre, so centimetres is the unit already on the page.
wrong.move: writes the area as seven centimetres, in a unit that measures a length.
wrong.screen: the unit card turns over under the count and shows one of the grid's squares lifted out, a centimetre along each side, labelled one square centimetre. A centimetre is laid beside it as an amber bar along one side only, and the seven squares are counted again, each lifting a moment as the card's square does. The child's answer stays in the slot with the unit keys lit.

wrong.why: the count is the part that took the work, and a number on its own looks finished.
wrong.move: gives the area as a bare number with no unit at all.
wrong.screen: the unit tag under the slot stays open and lit, and the same count is shown twice beside the shape, once as squares of this grid and once as squares of a grid twice as wide, the second drawing plainly bigger. The bare number fits both drawings, and the unit card names which squares were counted.

phases.screen: a shaded shape on a one-centimetre grid with the unit card face down
phases.soWhat: A square one centimetre on every side is one square centimetre, and an area is always written with a square unit.

phases.win: the rows fill down one at a time and the total lands as the rows times the row
phases.does: counts the first row, then copies it down and counts the rows
phases.goal: a shape of equal rows is counted as the rows times the squares in each
phases.says: How many in one row? How many rows? Put them together.
phases.check: A mat is covered by three rows of nine square tiles, each one unit on every side. What is its area? Say the rows first.
phases.feels: one row counted is every row counted, once you know how many rows there are
phases.hands: Draw a board of four rows of nine squares. Ask one child to count every square one by one while the class counts one row and then the rows. Ask which count finished first, and whether they agree.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many squares are in one row? Second rung, the phase's: how many rows are there, all the same? Third rung: the board is cut to two rows of three, and the rows control copies the first row down before the larger board comes back. The number pad and the unit keys stay open.

wrong.why: one row is counted with care, and the rows below it look like copies of something already counted.
wrong.move: counts one row and stops, giving seven for a tabletop covered in four rows of seven.
wrong.screen: the rows control copies the first row down one at a time, each new row lighting as it lands and the count of rows climbing beside it, until four rows stand. The total is written beside each row as it lands, seven, fourteen, twenty-one and twenty-eight, and the child's seven stays in the slot beside the first row.

wrong.why: two numbers put together has meant adding them for years, and both numbers are written side by side on the board.
wrong.move: adds the number of rows to the squares in one row, writing thirteen for six rows of seven.
wrong.screen: the rows fill down one at a time with the total beside each: seven, fourteen, twenty-one, twenty-eight, thirty-five and forty-two. The child's thirteen is laid out in tiles too, one row of seven with six more tiles standing below its first square, and the two coverings stand side by side, the thirteen leaving most of the board bare.

phases.screen: a rectangle on the sheet with one row of tiles laid and the rows control waiting
phases.soWhat: A covering of equal rows is counted by its rows, so four rows of seven squares is twenty-eight squares.
phases.concept: Rows instead of one by one

phases.win: the two counts stand side by side, one in square centimetres and one in centimetres, and they differ
phases.does: counts the squares inside with the tiles, then sends the edge walker round the outside
phases.goal: area counts the squares inside and perimeter measures the edge round them, and the two usually differ
phases.says: Count the squares inside. Now walk the edge. Are they the same number?
phases.check: Make a shape of five squares on squared paper. Find its area and its perimeter, each with its unit.
phases.feels: the squares inside and the edges round them are two counts of one shape, and they do not have to agree
phases.hands: Give each pair four paper squares of one size. Ask them to lay the four in a row, count the squares, and then count the edges round the outside with a finger. Then lay the same four as a square, two by two, and count both again. Ask which number changed and which did not.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: is the question asking for the squares inside or the edge round them? Second rung, the phase's: which unit goes with that? Third rung: the shape is cut to two squares side by side, and both counts are made before the larger shape comes back. The number pad and the unit keys stay open.

wrong.why: both numbers come off the same squares on the same grid, and counting squares is what this tool has been doing all along.
wrong.move: counts the squares when asked for the perimeter, giving six for a row of six squares whose edge is fourteen.
wrong.screen: the edge walker goes round the outside one square's edge at a time, each edge lighting amber as its count in the compare bay climbs to fourteen, while the tiles inside stay at six. The two counts stand side by side, one in square centimetres and one in centimetres, and the child's six stays in the slot under the edge count.

wrong.why: a longer way round seems to hold more inside it, and a long row looks bigger than a compact block.
wrong.move: expects the shape with the longer way round to have the bigger area, and picks a row of nine squares as bigger than a square three by three.
wrong.screen: the tiles are counted inside both shapes and the two counts land level, nine and nine, while the edge walker's counts beside them come out at twenty and twelve. The compare bay stands all four numbers in its two columns, the areas equal and the perimeters not, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a row of squares in the compare bay with both counts empty
phases.soWhat: Area counts the squares inside, in square units; perimeter measures the edge round them, in centimetres. They are different measures.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the rows control is pressed. The first row lifts a finger's width, a copy of it slides down beneath and snaps in, then another, then another, each landing with a soft click and its row number written at its left, while the total beside the board jumps by a whole row at every landing. When the last row lands the shape is covered edge to edge and the total stands still. It can be run again as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a shape lies on the squared sheet with its boundary drawn and its inside bare, and the tile tray is full under it. On the second a shape of shaded squares lies on a one-centimetre grid with the unit card face down under the running count. On the third a rectangle lies with its first row of tiles already laid and the rows control waiting at the right. On the fourth a row of squares stands in the compare bay with both its counts empty and the edge walker at one corner. The running count at the top left holds the tiles laid, none yet, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the top tile in the tray, or the face-down unit card, or the rows control, or the edge walker, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how much space is inside the shape. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any shape on the squared sheet, with the tiles, the rows control and the compare bay open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on covering with equal squares, square centimetres, counting by rows, and telling area from perimeter.
voiceLines: A shape on squared paper and a tray of equal squares. How much space is inside it?
Cover it with the squares. No gaps, and none on top of another.
Each square is one centimetre on every side. What unit is the area in?
How many in one row? How many rows? Put them together.
Count the squares inside. Now walk the edge. Are they the same number?
A new shape. Look at its rows before you count any squares.
Free play. Any shape on the sheet, with the tiles, the rows and the compare bay open.
Lift the tiles and lay them again one row at a time, counting aloud.
Every shape covered edge to edge, every area written with its unit, and every edge counted apart.

observations.why: Area counts the space inside once, so a gap would leave some out and an overlap would count some twice.
observations.soWhat: Equal squares laid edge to edge, with no gaps and no overlaps, are what make a count of squares an area.
observations.observe: A tile laid over a gap or on another tile sprang back and was never counted.

observations.why: The count is of squares, so the unit is a square as well.
observations.soWhat: An area is written in square units or square centimetres, never in centimetres.
observations.observe: The unit card turned over to show one square with each side a centimetre.

observations.why: Every row of a rectangle holds the same number of squares.
observations.soWhat: Count one row and the number of rows, and the covering is counted without touching every square.
observations.observe: The rows control copied one row down, and the total grew by a whole row at each landing.

observations.why: The squares inside and the edge round them are different things, one a space and the other a length.
observations.soWhat: Area and perimeter are different measures of a shape, and finding one does not give the other.
observations.observe: For the row of squares and for the square block alike, the edge count and the square count came out different.

source_tool.description: A shape is drawn on a squared sheet, and a tray of equal square tiles sits beside it. Tiles are dragged onto the shape and snap edge to edge; a tile laid across a gap or on top of another is handed back with the gap or the overlap lit, so the covering has no gaps and no overlaps. A counter at the top left of the canvas counts the tiles as they land, and a unit card under it reads square units, or square centimetres once the sheet's squares are marked as one centimetre on every side. A rows control fills one row of a rectangle, then copies it down row by row, counting the rows and the squares in each, so the total is built from rows rather than one square at a time. A compare bay sets two counts side by side for one shape: the squares inside it, counted by the tiles, and the edges round it, counted by a small walker that goes round the outside one square edge at a time.
source_tool.art_direction: Square tiles on a squared sheet / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a drawing board with a ruler and a point stamp, a tracing finger and a flag, a walker and a string, square tiles on squared paper, a pair of compasses with a metal point and a pencil arm, a sheet of paper that folds, an upright mirror, solids on a turntable, flat nets that fold up, hinged arms, a clock face and a grid of pictures.

A line is always drawn with an arrowhead at each end, a ray with a dot at its end point and one arrowhead, and a line segment with a dot at each end. No stroke is ever left with a bare end that could be read as either.

A point is drawn as one small dot of one size wherever it appears, named by a capital letter beside it. Within one figure no letter ever names two different things, and a figure never renames a part it has already named.

Every labelled length is one the figure could really have, and every figure is drawn to scale with its labels. A triangle drawn with a square corner carries lengths such as three, four and five, and a stepped shape's sides close up exactly.
A figure on squared paper sits exactly on the grid lines, with every side along a line and every square either wholly inside it or wholly outside it.

A circle drawn to show its parts has its centre marked as a dot and named. Every radius is drawn from that dot to the curve, and a diameter always passes exactly through the dot. A circle that is a view of a solid carries a dot only where the solid has a point, so a cylinder seen from above is a plain circle.
A right angle carries a small square corner mark, and every other angle an arc drawn close to its vertex between the arms.

A line of symmetry and a mirror line are drawn dotted and lie exactly where the fold falls. A fold line being tried is drawn solid and turns dotted only once the fold is kept. Every mirror line stands upright unless the frame says it lies across, and an image sits exactly as far behind the line as the thing in front of it, turned the other way round.
A solid is drawn with its hidden edges dashed. Views of one solid are drawn at one scale, so the front view and the side view of a box are exactly the same height.

Clock hands point exactly at the numbers and the minute hand is the longer. Where the angle between the hands is shown, both angles are shaded and the smaller one is outlined. No clock is set to six o'clock or twelve o'clock.
A grid carries its row numbers down the left edge and its column numbers across the top, and each picture in it appears once.
A shape, a side or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a line, a point, a square or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that opens on the point cannot afford a frame where a point has to be hunted for. A length being measured, walked, added or named, the tape, the walker's sum, a radius being measured, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted, so a dotted line always means a true line of symmetry. Sky blue is the second thing set beside the first: a fold being tried, drawn solid until it is kept, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter, and the larger angle between clock hands. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because a point is a round dot, a measured length carries its number, a line of symmetry is dotted, a fold being tried is solid and a hidden edge is dashed.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

phase_map.concept: Rows instead of one by one

placement.where: After a book cover has been covered with paper squares of one size, edge to edge, and counted. The tool is what refuses a tile laid over a gap or on another tile, and sets the squares inside beside the edges round, which squared paper leaves the child to keep apart alone.

answer_key.rule: Area is the amount of space inside the boundary of a shape, found by covering it with equal squares that meet edge to edge, with no gaps and no overlaps, and counting them. It is written in square units, and when each square is one centimetre on every side, in square centimetres. A shape made of equal rows can be counted by rows: the number of rows times the number of squares in each. Area and perimeter measure different things: the area counts the squares inside, and the perimeter measures the length of the edge round them, so the two numbers usually differ.
answer_key.wrong: The tiles are lifted and laid again one row at a time with the count said aloud, and any gap or overlap is lit where it sits. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The tiles are equal squares that cover the book completely, with no gaps and no overlaps.
So counting them counts the space inside the boundary: there are eighteen.
Each tile is one square unit, so the area is eighteen square units.
items.question: A book cover is covered with equal square tiles, each one unit on every side. Eighteen tiles fit, edge to edge, with no gaps and none on top of another. What is the area of the cover?
items.checkpoint: Area is the space inside a boundary, counted in equal squares with no gaps and no overlaps.
items.misconception: Counting tiles that overlap or leaving gaps, or writing the answer with no unit.

steps: Each square on the grid is one centimetre on every side, so each is one square centimetre.
Two rows of three make six squares, and one more makes seven.
So the area is seven square centimetres, written with a square unit.
items.question: On a one-centimetre grid, a shape covers two rows of three squares and one more square below them. What is its area?
items.checkpoint: A square one centimetre on every side gives one square centimetre.
items.misconception: Writing the answer as seven centimetres, which is a length and not an area.

steps: Each row has seven squares, and there are six rows, all the same.
Six rows of seven make forty-two squares, without counting them one by one.
Each square is one square centimetre, so the area is forty-two square centimetres.
items.question: A board is marked in six rows of seven squares, each square one centimetre on every side. What is its area?
items.checkpoint: A shape of equal rows is counted as the rows times the squares in each row.
items.misconception: Adding six and seven to get thirteen instead of counting six rows of seven.

steps: Count the squares inside: six, so the area is six square centimetres.
Walk the edge: six centimetres along the top, one down the end, six along the bottom and one up the other end.
Six, one, six and one make fourteen, so the perimeter is fourteen centimetres, a different number.
items.answer: The area is six square centimetres and the perimeter is fourteen centimetres
items.question: Six squares, each one centimetre on every side, sit in one row. Find the area and the perimeter of the row.
items.checkpoint: Area counts the squares inside and perimeter measures the edge round them.
items.misconception: Giving the same number for both because both were counted on the same squares.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A mat is covered by twenty-four equal square tiles of side one unit, with no gaps and no overlaps. What is its area?
Two tiles on a floor lie partly on top of each other. Why does that spoil the count of the area?
items.final_answer: The space where they overlap is counted twice, so the tiles must meet edge to edge with no overlaps

items.question: Five squares of a one-centimetre grid are shaded. What is the area of the shaded part?
A shaded shape on a one-centimetre grid has a row of five squares with a row of four below it. What is its area?
A board has nine rows of nine squares, each one centimetre on every side. What is its area?
items.final_answer: Eighty-one square centimetres, because nine rows of nine make eighty-one

items.question: A path is laid with square tiles of side one unit, in five rows of eight. How many square units does it cover?
items.final_answer: Forty square units, because five rows of eight make forty

items.question: A rectangle on a one-centimetre grid is three squares long and two squares wide. Find its area and its perimeter.
items.final_answer: The area is six square centimetres and the perimeter is ten centimetres

items.question: One shape is a square three squares by three. Another is nine squares in one row. Each square is one centimetre on every side. Compare their areas and their perimeters.
items.final_answer: Both have an area of nine square centimetres, but the square's perimeter is twelve centimetres and the row's is twenty centimetres

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds equal square tiles to drag onto the shape
sets each tile edge to edge with the one beside it
hands back a tile over a gap or on another tile, with the place lit
counts the tiles at the top left of the canvas
reads square units, or square centimetres for one-centimetre squares
fills one row and copies it down, counting the rows and the squares in each
goes round the outside one square edge at a time, counting
sets the squares inside beside the edges round for one shape

teaching_notes: Cover a real book with paper squares before the tool is opened, edge to edge, and count them. Then cover it again with squares of a bigger size, and let the class find that the count changed while the book did not; the squares must be one size for the count to mean anything. The page's tabletop is four rows of seven, twenty-eight squares, and its shaded shape is two rows of four, eight square centimetres; read both off together before anything is tiled here. Count by rows as early as possible. A chessboard counted one square at a time loses its place, and eight rows of eight does not. Keep the unit in every answer. Area is in square units or square centimetres because it counts squares, and the moment a child writes centimetres for an area, the compare bay shows that centimetres belong to the edge. The squared figures in the perimeter exercise are the best test of the difference: for every one of them the perimeter and the area are different numbers, so a child who counts squares when asked for the edge is caught at once.
generation_prompt: Build an area tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A shape is drawn on a squared sheet in the working area, every side along a grid line and every square wholly inside or wholly outside it. A tray of equal square tiles sits beside the sheet; a tile dragged onto the shape snaps edge to edge with its neighbours, and a tile dropped across a gap or onto another tile springs back to the tray with the gap or the overlap lit, nothing marked. A tile counter at the top left of the canvas counts tiles as they land, and a unit card beneath it reads square units, or square centimetres once the sheet is marked as one-centimetre squares. A rows control fills one row of a rectangle, then copies it down one row at a time, showing the number of rows and the number in each row beside the growing total. A compare bay at the right sets two counts for one shape side by side: the squares inside it, counted by the tiles, and the edges round it, counted by a small walker that goes round the outside one square edge at a time and reports in centimetres. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Cover the shape with squares, edge to edge. Leave no gaps and put none on top of another. Count the squares. Write the area in square units. Count by rows when you can.
